rows.title: Osaka vs Rybakina
rows.tournament: US Open R4 (round of 16), outdoor hard, Louis Armstrong Stadium
rows.headline: Rybakina is the better hard-court player and beat Osaka a month ago, but both are hurt
rows.analysis: US Open R4 on Armstrong, not before 2:30pm ET Monday. Rybakina (#2, 42-13, AO champion, IW and Toronto finalist) beat Osaka (#13) 4-6 7-6(5) 6-4 in Toronto four weeks ago in the same conditions, but had to save four break points at 3-2 in the third and made 72 unforced errors, so Osaka's flat, early-taken ball clearly troubles her. Osaka is 0-2 against top-10 players on hard courts this year (1-7 overall, the only win on grass at Wimbledon) and has laboured through this draw: two tiebreaks without a break of serve vs #102 Zakharova, three sets vs #39 Siniakova, then 2h38 vs #20 Mertens with a medical timeout on her chronic left Achilles at 3-4 in the decider ('shocked I won'). Rybakina has not dropped a set (6-3 6-2, 6-2 6-4, 7-6(6) 6-3) though she was broken at 4-4 and saved a set point vs #74 Starodubtseva, and her left heel tendon (retired Cincinnati QF Aug 21, seven days off, mixed doubles withdrawn) is felt most on the serve landing. Hard-court chains lean Rybakina: same-week Miami she beat Gibson 6-2 6-2 while Osaka lost to her; Rybakina went 1-2 in tight matches with Sabalenka while Osaka lost 2-6 4-6 at IW. Two wins from World No.1 is a real carrot. Both are compromised, so this stays near a coin flip: Rybakina about 59%, no medal.

Bernet is also 0-2 against lefties this year, and a lefty forehand into a one-handed backhand on clay is a real pattern. Market has Dedura 1.66 (~56%); I land at 58%. rows.title: Kawahashi vs Ryan Ziegann
rows.tournament: Phan Thiet 3 Challenger (CH50) final qualifying round, outdoor hard, Phan Thiet, Vietnam
rows.headline: Ziegann beat him 6 weeks ago; Kawahashi 1-6 since a July retirement, fading after set one
rows.analysis: Final qualifying round at the Phan Thiet 3 Challenger, outdoor hard, first on Court A at 10:00 local (03:00 UTC, not Kalshi's 06:00). Books make Kawahashi 1.61 on ranking (#663 v #820) and his stronger 2025 (M15 title, three finals, 42-22), but 2026 tells a different story: he is 7-12, and since retiring 0-6 0-5 down at Wuning on Jul 7 he is 1-6. His three completed losses since (Ziegann, Qian Sun, #1179 qualifier Tanuma) all had the same shape: won the first set comfortably, then lost the next two with the decider 6-3, 6-0 and 6-1. That is a physical or concentration fade, not variance, and his only win since was 6-2 6-1 over a Nepali wildcard. Ziegann, 191cm with a big serve, is at his career-high level, has been in these SE-Asian conditions since Jul 20 (10-3 outdoors, M15 Bali 2 final on Aug 2, three sets with #550 Borg on Sep 4) and already came from 1-6 down to beat Kawahashi in Bali. Against that, the older common-opponent chains (Meng 6-0 6-1, Zhu M., Tanuma margin) say a healthy Kawahashi is the better player, and Ziegann throws in bad days (6-3 6-1 to #990 Oh indoors two weeks ago). Slight Ziegann lean at 55%, below the bronze bar.

rows.headline: Thai teen loses close to ~#1000 players; Ikeda gets routed by unranked ones
rows.analysis: Two of the weakest players on the ITF circuit meet in Nonthaburi qualifying, so the read is who loses less badly. Khantiweerawat is 0-4 in 2026 and 6-38 for his career, but every 2026 defeat was close and to a real player: 5-7 4-6 to Oh Chan-Yeong (#1006, 21-13 this year), 2-6 4-6 to Trongcharoenchaikul (#986), 6-1 2-6 7-10 to Pantaratorn (#1838) and 5-7 3-6 to Sato, who then qualified. He also took Meng Fanming (now #1027) to 9-11 in a deciding tiebreak last December. Ikeda (4-13 in 2026, 18-68 career) beat three unranked no-hopers this year but was routed 6-1 6-1 by #1856 Tange and 6-2 6-3 by #1360 Muto, and lost to unranked players with 4-14 and 2-6 career records; his one good result is pushing Arcon (#1502) to 7-10 last week. The only cross-chain (Meng beat Arcon 6-2 6-4, Arcon edged Ikeda, Meng barely beat Khantiweerawat) leans Thai. Add home courts and heat he plays in every week, a 19-year-old's upward trend against a 26-year-old journeyman, and books moving from 1.64 to about 1.47 on him. Still a coin flip with a lean: he rarely closes matches and Ikeda's best form is his most recent.

Lee, back in April after a 10-month layoff, went 22-3 on hard in Asia with two W15 titles and a W35 semi, beating Chanta (#414) twice and Cheapchandej (#477) twice; her 5-6 European swing was entirely on clay, her weakest surface, and includes an ugly 1-6 3-6 loss to #1034 Ivanovic two weeks ago as a 1.35 favourite. Vlasselaer, 25 and drifting from a 398 high, is 10-9 on outdoor hard in 2026 with wins only over #800-plus or unranked opponents and losses to Griffiths (#1116) and unranked Dilek on Portuguese hard; she has not played in 26 days and lost first-up after a similar August gap last year. Books opened Vlasselaer 1.55 and have drifted to 1.68 with Lee 2.00, so money is moving toward Lee and Kalshi already leans her. Lean Lee, a coin flip with a feather.

rows.headline: Blockx's serve vs Cerundolo's weak return, plus a 7.5-hour fatigue gap, tips a close one
rows.analysis: US Open R16, Monday Sep 7 (order of play not yet published; Kalshi's Sep 6 is a day early). Books: Blockx 1.60 / Cerundolo 2.33, matching Kalshi. Blockx is the pick at ~60%. The matchup is the core: Cerundolo's return has struggled vs big servers all week (23% first-return points vs Struff, 30% vs Fritz, 2/12 break points vs Fritz) and both wins needed five sets; Blockx, 6'4", won 86% of first-serve points with 17 aces vs Cobolli and saved 8/8 break points beating Cerundolo 7-6(8) 6-2 in Madrid. Fatigue is asymmetric: Cerundolo has 7h33 on court over two five-setters in three days (his Feb lumbar retirement came after a similar overload) vs Blockx's 2h45 four-setter and two routine wins. Blockx is 14-9 in 2026 tiebreaks, Cerundolo 5-9. Against that, Cerundolo's hard-court ceiling is higher (Rublev, Medvedev, Humbert, Fritz beaten this year), he is 2-0 in fifth sets this week while Blockx has never played one at a Slam, and Blockx blew 5-3 serving for the Cincinnati match vs Cobolli. rows.title: Medvedev vs Tiafoe
rows.tournament: US Open R4 (round of 16), outdoor hard, Louis Armstrong Stadium, New York
rows.headline: Medvedev's return game has owned Tiafoe (6-0 on hard), serve is back; Tiafoe nursing issues
rows.analysis: Genuinely close, and the market (Kalshi 58%, tennisexplorer 1.63/2.27, Matchbook 1.71/2.40, hard-court Elo ~55%) has it about right. Case for Tiafoe: the best summer of his career (Cincinnati final beating Auger-Aliassime #4, Musetti, Nakashima, Tien), 40 wins in 2026, a dominant R3 (never broken, 85% first-serve points), home crowd on Armstrong, and recent same-surface chains that lean his way (he beat Nakashima, Damm and Tien within the month Medvedev lost to all three). Case for Medvedev, which I weigh slightly heavier: the matchup evidence is overwhelming and current-season, 6-0 in tour main draws on hard with one set dropped, including 6-3 6-2 in 61 minutes in January without facing a break point; his deep return and consistency turn Tiafoe's serve-forehand game into long rallies Tiafoe loses. His August slump (van de Zandschulp, Nakashima with 3 MPs, Damm) has visibly turned: 9-0 in sets here, broken once, big serving numbers vs Rinderknech. Tiafoe has had a cyst removed from his right wrist (Aug 8), a hip MTO in the Cincy final, withdrew from mixed doubles, played a 3h48 five-setter in R1, and on Sep 4 acknowledged he is managing physical problems and wants shorter matches; that is exactly the wrong profile against a grinder in best-of-five. Lean Medvedev ~59%, no medal: Tiafoe's form and the chains are real counter-evidence and Medvedev has folded from winning positions three times since June.

Common opponents lean Senica (Hrdinkova, Meyer auf der Heide, Ceuca) while the freshest same-surface chain via Grubor leans Mrazikova, so the chains roughly cancel. Both are clay-only players, both played three matches with one three-setter, neither is in doubles, no injury signs found. Bookmakers 1.57/2.20 (about 58% Senica) match Kalshi. I make Senica about 57%: the more proven player at this level, but a coin-flip lean, not a conviction, so no medal.

Gannon (#826, career high, 1.85m right-hander with a big serve, 18 aces in the Dublin final) has the higher ceiling: since June he beat Tomic (#192) at the Dublin Challenger, won M15 Dublin over De Jonge (#568) and Molder (#843), and yesterday beat #493 Boogaard 7-6(2) 6-2 as a 4.31 underdog. Against that: Javia is fresher (Gannon played singles plus a three-set doubles SF yesterday in 38C), fully acclimatised, and a windy 09:00 start rewards his steadier baseline game. Lazarenko is the counter: three hard-court W15 titles in 2026, 17-5 in doubles, singles SF here and a 6-4 3-6 6-2 singles win over Sharabura on Wednesday. rows.analysis: Verified as US Open WD second round, first match on Stadium 17 at 11am ET Saturday (15:00Z, not Kalshi's 18:00Z); NWS says sunny, no rain. Books are pick'em (1.82/1.81 tennisexplorer, 1.91/1.80 tennisstats) while Kalshi has Routliffe/Sutjiadi at 46-47c, so the pick is also the cheaper side. Routliffe/Sutjiadi have partnered on and off since 2021, won DC in July without dropping a set, went 9-2 on this hard-court swing (losses only to Mihalikova/Nicholls and eventual Cincy champs Bouzkova/Noskova 7-5 7-5) and beat Li/Tauson 6-2 6-2 with one unforced error. Fernandez/Tjen is a brand-new pairing; their 6-1 6-1 R1 came against an ITF-level pair. Same-week DC chains point one way: R/S routed Tang/Xu and Klepac/Ninomiya, who beat Danilina/Fernandez and Tjen/Zhang. Fernandez is ~8-12 in 2026 doubles with 10 partners and Routliffe's pairs are 3-0 against hers. Counter-evidence is real: Tjen is a genuine doubles talent (5 titles since Sep 2025, beat Sutjiadi's pair in Auckland and Fernandez's pair in Abu Dhabi), the lefty/righty return combo can attack Sutjiadi's serve, and Routliffe's 2026 outside DC was poor. Fernandez's 2h10 singles loss Friday is rhythm, not fatigue. Lean R/S ~56%; no medal, the reasons are solid but not independent enough or strong enough for 0.62.

Results evidence also leans Italian: B/V beat Heliovaara/Patten twice this year (Miami final 6-4 6-2 on hard) while H/H lost to them twice in straights, and B/V beat Herbert/Mahut 7-6(2) 6-2 at RG 2025. Against that, B/V are 4-4 since Wimbledon (two losses to Luz/Matos, one to lucky losers) and H/H's two big serves make tiebreaks likely. H/H are 1-4 in their last five though and lost 4-6 2-6 to Frantzen/Haase last week. Weather dry and cooler. I make it ~62% B/V, bronze on two independent factors.

rows.title: Zheng vs Gea
rows.tournament: US Open R3 (round of 32), outdoor hard, Grandstand, New York
rows.headline: Gea beat Zheng twice on hard this year from a set down; near coin flip, lean the 2.2 dog
rows.analysis: US Open R3, third match on Grandstand Saturday (day session from 11am ET, so est. 2:30-3:30pm ET / ~19:00 UTC). Books: Zheng 1.66-1.68, Gea 2.21-2.26; Kalshi 57/43. I make it a near coin flip and lean Gea. The only direct matchup evidence favours him: 2-0 on hard this year, both times after Zheng won the first set (Noumea SF 4-6 6-1 6-4; Los Cabos R16 0-6 6-4 6-0 as a +154 dog). In Los Cabos Zheng landed 45% of first serves and won 46% of second-serve points; Gea won 45% of return games. Gea is the higher-ranked player (#87 vs #107), is roughly 22-4 on hard in 2026 with an ATP title and wins over Lehecka, F. Cerundolo and Shapovalov, and closes matches brutally (6-0/6-1 final sets vs Zheng, F. Cerundolo, J.M. Cerundolo). Zheng's case is real: 81-83% first-serve points and 27/31 holds this fortnight, 22 aces, a home Grandstand crowd, and cool dry weather unlike the Los Cabos heat. Gea also showed variance, losing 3-6 1-6 to #163 Basavareddy in Q3 eight days ago. But Zheng's holds came against poor returners (Marozsan, Bu) and Gea returns far better. Transitive chains are thin and cancel; no fatigue or injury factor for either. A lean, not a conviction.

rows.analysis: US Open R3, Sat Sep 5, second on Armstrong after the 11:00 ET opener (est. 13:00 ET / 17:00 UTC). Books: Cobolli -110 (1.80-1.85), Blockx +100 (1.92-1.95). Cobolli (#6, RG finalist, Wimbledon QF, Cincinnati SF with wins over Paul #21 and Jodar #13) is the better player and the format helps him: best-of-five dilutes Blockx's serving streaks, and Cobolli is 13-2 at slams this year while Blockx is in his first slam third round. On faster Cincinnati courts Cobolli won 7-5 4-6 7-5 from 3-5 down in the decider; Blockx landed only 51% first serves and won 51% of second-serve points, and he was again at 51% first serves vs Trungelliti, so the second serve is there for Cobolli's return. Blockx has no top-30 hard-court win in 2026 (tour-level hard 3-4; his Madrid/Estoril surge was on clay), and NYC conditions (ace rate 8.7%, heavy humid balls, 83F day session) tilt toward attrition tennis. The honest counter: Cobolli has 6h55 on court from two slow-starting matches, calls himself 'slightly more tired', and in 2025 retired in this exact round after long early matches; Blockx is fresher, hit 27 aces in two rounds and was two points from beating him in Cincy. The direct evidence points to Jovic: 2-0 this year with dominant margins, including 6-2 6-2 on grass at Queen's when Eala was in form (she beat Swiatek three weeks later), plus a 6-3 exhibition set on this exact court nine days ago. The mechanism repeats: Jovic takes the ball early, out-hits Eala from the baseline (34-15 and 26-12 winners) and attacks Eala's weak serve, while her own serve is clearly better (67% first-serve points won, 5 aces v Frech). Eala's 2026 hard-court ledger shows the same vulnerability to flat power righties: blown out by Noskova, Muchova, Bencic (4-6 0-6), Gauff, Alexandrova and Anisimova. The counter-case is real: hard is Eala's best surface (25-10), her DC title run over Pegula, Svitolina and Osaka gives her much stronger hard-court transitive chains, Elo favours her, and Jovic's summer hard results were soft (lost to #89 Korneeva and Bouzkova, 26 UE v Jones). Deden is a 25-year-old Dutch coach with his own tennis school, #40 on the Dutch national list, who played Eredivisie league on clay this spring for Lauswolt (lost 6-0 6-3 to Robin Haase, a tight two-setter to Leimonias). His entire pro singles record is 4-3 in Haren/Alkmaar qualifying, but he beats unranked Dutch players routinely and was 7-6(7) 7-5 from Hendrikx (#2176) on these courts a year ago. He is a wildcard here (no qualifying played) and won doubles R16 Tuesday. Blando is a doubles specialist (#857, 5'11 140lb, spin serves, formation play) with a 5-18 pro singles record before this week; his three Q wins were a 10-7 tiebreak over a German who is 1-4 this year, a one-set retirement, and Waterbolk (#2087, 9-19 in 2026). He loses in straights to anyone ranked 1000-1750. Slow, damp evening clay after afternoon rain suits the home baseliner more than Blando's net game. Against that, Blando is match-tough on these exact courts and Deden has not played ITF singles in 12 months. Deden ~56%, but neither side is buyable at the current asks. Start slipped from the 15:00 UTC slot; Sofascore now lists 17:00 UTC and the match had not started at 16:22 UTC.

Wind of 12-25 mph is forecast, which helps the steadier man. Net: Friend about 54%, which is the market. No mispricing found, no medal.

rows.analysis: Zhangjiagang R16, first match on Court 6 at 11:00 local (03:00 UTC, not Kalshi's 06:00). Books have Hsu 1.56-1.58 / Trotter 2.2-2.32 (fair ~59% Hsu); Kalshi asks 0.63. Hsu (#268, CH 158) is a steady Challenger QF-level player: Winnipeg QF in July losing only to eventual champion Samuel (#110), an M25 Taipei title in August beating Dellavedova (#293), then R1 here 7-6(4) 5-5 when Ymer (#204) collapsed in the heat. Trotter (#464, CH 170) has cratered in 2026: he retired at Gwangju qualifying in April, missed seven weeks, lost two Futures matches in June, went 0-3 in Canadian Challenger main draws (Chidekh 6-1 6-2, Draxl, Zink), then sat out all of August before beating wildcard Cui (#454) 6-3 6-4 as a pick'em. His only 2026 win over anyone inside #350 is Matsuoka (#250) in Vancouver qualifying. H2H is 1-1, but Hsu's 6-3 6-3 Busan win came in Apr 2025 with Trotter at his career-high; Trotter's Yokkaichi 2023 win was on faster Japanese hard. Transitive chain via Moriya (Hsu won 6-2 6-3, Trotter lost) leans Hsu. Trotter has one extra rest day and a live serve (10 aces vs Cui), and Hsu has had bad losses (Gorzny #876, Mmoh), so 65% is the ceiling. No unpriced factor found: everything here is on public result pages, so no medal.

rows.title: Forti vs Clarke
rows.tournament: Como Lake Challenger R32 (Challenger 75), Como, Italy, outdoor clay
rows.headline: Clarke's class, clay pedigree and H2H win at a coin-flip price books make 52/48
rows.analysis: Official OOP: 3rd on Court 1 from 10:00 CEST (~11:30 UTC est). Books price Clarke 1.77 v Forti 1.92 (~52% no-vig); Kalshi is 50/50. The retail read — home Italian clay grinder v traveling Brit — inverts under research: clay is Clarke's BEST surface (189-102 career, 3 M25 clay titles in 2024, two at Santa Margherita di Pula), and he beat Forti 7-6(3) 6-3 on that same Italian Futures circuit in May 2023 when Forti was near his career-high level. Clarke's ugly 20-26 season is losses to top-200 players (Sakamoto #157 who then beat Muller, Chidekh #176, Kym #186 — all 3-setters); v #300+ opposition he mostly wins, and Forti is #363. Forti's comeback from a foot double bone oedema (#600 in March to #363) is real but Futures-padded (~8-9 Challenger MD wins); his last meeting with a Clarke-ranked opponent ended 6-1 6-3 to Cecchinato (#195) three weeks ago, and he retired from a Futures match Aug 18 before playing quali here. Forti's court time in Como and home crowd keep this close, but at equal 50c I side with the sharper book lean, class and H2H. Clarke ~53%.

Misasi (25, #859 = career high) made the Curtea de Arges final Aug 9, is 7-3 in his last 10, and his only losses are to better-ranked in-form players (Ghetu #625 as a 4.03 dog, ex-Challenger Madaras, title-winner Pieleanu #764); he routinely crushes lower-ranked youngsters (6-0 6-0, 6-1 6-2, 6-3 6-3 this month) — exactly Breazu's current profile. But Yao arrives off a 5-losses-in-7 German clay swing, beaten by #390 Schunk 6-0 4-6... incl. #504 McAdoo and #727 Wobker, and hasn't won a hard-court match since June 7. Kulikova's most recent tennis is a 5-0 W75 Lexington title run on hard (beat #293 Akli in the final) after qualifying into the Figueira WTA 125, where she beat #167 Hontama — the same Hontama who bageled Yao's second set six days earlier on Chinese hard and also beat Yao in Sep 2025. Both come in rested (~3-4 weeks idle); Kulikova's 29-day layoff plus US-to-China travel is the main drag on her, Yao has been home since mid-August. Chains and current level favor Kulikova modestly; home comfort, surface base and H2H favor Yao. I make it a slight Kulikova lean at 53% vs a 49c ask.

Choi, 19, is at a career-high ~#1045 and 20-14 in 2026 with a W15 QF on outdoor hard at Luan in July; she is the top qualifying seed and won her only quali match 6-4 6-3. Shin, 24, is now a doubles player (#671 doubles vs #1284 singles, career-high #862 long past): 12-13 in 2026 with wins mostly over Q-1R fodder, a mid-match retirement Aug 2, a 6-1 6-1 quali loss Aug 9, and a 10-8 match-tiebreak escape vs Eom on Sunday after two matches that day. rows.analysis: Borg (#536, CH #334) is the classier player: 7 ITF titles, won M15 Ahmedabad on hard in March and QF'd Islamabad on hard in April, and he just won 4 matches reaching the Bastad final. But that run was at his home club on clay vs a weak Swedish field (he blew a set lead in the final vs #1054 Guttau, and before Bastad he'd lost 4 straight 1R matches). He flew Sweden→Bali this week off that Aug 23 final — first hard court in 4 months, first tropical midday match since May. Chang (#1296, ex-Cal All-Pac-12) has played at Bali Beach CC itself for six straight weeks: M15 Bali legs 1-2 in July, where he lost only razor-thin 3-setters to ranked vets Takahashi 7-6(8)-in-the-3rd and Boosarawongse, then 9-1 through the UTR PTT events, winning the title Aug 23 on Court A. His ranking badly lags his level (thin pro schedule, 40-26 career). Pinnacle's vig-free line is Borg 61/Chang 39; I shade to 57/43 for venue immersion, acclimatization and Borg's transition. That makes Chang at Kalshi's 40c ask slightly +EV and Borg at 63c overpriced. Small, honest edge — bronze.

rows.tournament: Plovdiv 3 Challenger (CH50) R32, outdoor red clay, Plovdiv, Bulgaria
rows.headline: Rising clay-only #357 vs #643 qualifier whose 2026 wins came on hard; 51c is fair-cheap
rows.analysis: Books (Estevez 1.77-1.83 vs 1.92-1.88) and Kalshi price this as a coin flip, but the profiles diverge on this surface. Estevez, 20, is a pure clay grinder (35-23 in 2026, all clay) with a real Challenger clay final in June at Asuncion (beat Huertas del Pino, lost 7-6 4-6 2-6 to Hardt) and the best scalp of either player's last month: #250 Nedic from a set down at Augsburg. His Euro-trip losses were all competitive against better or hotter opponents (Blancaneaux ~#400 7-5 in the third; Sanchez Martinez during a maiden-CH-SF heater). Iannaccone, 27, built his 2026 on hard courts (Cesenatico CH QF, Hersonissos R16); on clay he is ~7-6 with zero Challenger MD clay wins and 2026 clay losses to Krutykh #526, Jorda Sanchis, Martin Manzano and Nesterov. He also sat out 7+ weeks (Jul 1-Aug 23) and plays a third straight day, though two qualifying wins give him rhythm and court acclimation Estevez lacks. Net: Estevez ~56% vs the 51c ask - a modest lean, not a mispricing; everything above is on public activity pages, so no medal.

rows.headline: 2-0 H2H on hard plus a 21cm serve edge; market over-discounts one bad M15 week
rows.analysis: Zhangjiagang Challenger 75, R1, outdoor hard, second on Court 6. Official draw sheet (released 31 Aug) has Bar Biryukov as the #8 seed at #286; Leong is a qualifier at #551. The decisive fact is a verified 2-0 H2H, both on hard: BB won 6-2 5-7 6-3 in the Bengaluru Open III QF in May en route to the title (beat Ivashka in the final), and 7-5 6-4 at a 2025 Futures. Style backs it: BB is a 196cm lefty, Leong 175cm right-handed, and Leong's season losses cluster against bigger hitters (Castelnuovo x2, Skatov, Shin 6-2 6-2). The market has already discounted BB hard (1.53-1.56, ~59%) for a poor month: 1R M15 loss to unranked Qian Sun 6-3 6-4 on Aug 26, a 6-4 6-2 Challenger loss to Cui Jie, a mid-match retirement Aug 4. That discount looks a touch too large: a #286 with a 2-0 same-surface H2H over a #551 qualifier should sit nearer 63-65%. Transitive chains are genuinely even (both lost 3-setters to Simakin, both beat Huang Tsung-Hao). Leong is sharper and heat-adapted (32C, humid) but plays a third straight day and his qualy wins came over #496 Palan plus a retirement.

He returned from a wrist layoff at UTR PTT Bali on Aug 17, beat Thomas Patton 6-4 7-5, then withdrew from his next match on Aug 18 when the wrist flared again (Sofascore logs a walkover; antaranews and viva name the injury). He is a home wildcard here and also plays doubles R16 with Ellis the same day. Perez Ramos is #953, at a career high set Aug 3, 21-6 in singles in 2026 all on hard with two Futures finals and a SF, and he beat Shanker Heisnam - the #3 seed in this event's qualifying - 6-2 6-4 in May. He is ruthless against sub-level fields (6-0 6-3, 6-1 6-0, 6-3 6-3). Against that, he has not played since a flat Aug 4 loss to Coquelin at M25 Roehampton and must arrive into Nusa Dua heat and humidity from Europe, while Barki is acclimatised and has played this venue repeatedly. Rust and a home crowd are the genuine counterweights and ITF first rounds are chaotic, but the level gap plus a wrist that failed 14 days ago is the bigger fact. No bookmaker has priced this match at all.

rows.analysis: M25 Urayasu (SBC Dream Tennis, $30k outdoor hard, Chiba), R32, Sept 1. Lee is the 6th seed, #616, 17-16 in 2026 and runner-up at M25 Ma'anshan in April (l. Alastair Gray 2-6 3-6) — a genuine M25-level player. Katayama is a 37-year-old home wildcard, #1523, 170cm, Japan's domestic #41; TennisExplorer lists ZERO singles matches for him in 2026 and his last singles match was Matsuyama Challenger in Nov 2025. He also lost the only H2H (2017 Futures final). Taipei→Tokyo travel after a typhoon-compressed week is a real but small drag. Common opponents (Ochi, Hazawa) lean Lee. Lee ~70% — but at a 90c ask this is not a buy.

rows.title: Cerundolo vs Gea
rows.tournament: US Open R1 (men's singles), outdoor hard (Laykold), Flushing Meadows NY — Court 6, 3rd match, best-of-5
rows.headline: Gea's 2026 hard-court resume beats a clay-built lefty who is 1-3 in hard slam main draws
rows.analysis: First meeting, priced as a coin flip and it nearly is. Cerundolo (#45) is 42 spots higher but his ranking is clay-built: Bordeaux Challenger title, RG R16 off a cramping Sinner, and just 1-3 lifetime in hard-court slam main draws. On hard in 2026 he is 7-5, best win Rinderknech in two tiebreaks, and he was blown out by Ruud (1-6 2-6) and Auger-Aliassime (5-7 1-6). Gea is ~13-3 on hard in 2026 with wins over Lehecka (best-of-5 at the AO), Francisco Cerundolo and Shapovalov en route to the Los Cabos title, is 31-12 on hard vs 14-14 on clay at CH/ITF level, and is 2-1 vs lefties on hard this year. That surface-quality gap is the lean. Against it: Gea played zero matches Aug 1-23, then lost the final qualifying round 3-6 1-6 to #156 Basavareddy on these courts serving badly, and best-of-5 in mid-80s humidity is the grinder's arena — Cerundolo has 8 tour hard matches in 17 days and elite stamina. Those offset most, not all, of it. The book opened Gea 1.68 and has drifted to 1.82 (52.3%); Kalshi matches it. I make him ~55%. Thin value at 52c, no mispricing to point at.

His 6-1 6-3 and 6-1 6-1 qualifying wins look dominant but came against #625 Prajwal Dev and a lower-ranked Lomakin - the kind of form signal a naive model over-weights. Best shared read is Wu Tung-Lin: Moriya is 0-2 v him in 2026 including 2-6 2-6 at Futures level ten days ago, while Samrej beat Wu in a Shanghai Challenger main draw. Against that, Samrej was blown out 1-6 2-6 by Dellavedova in a Futures semi two days ago (4th match in 4 days) then travelled from Taipei, and sits at his season-low ranking. Thin edge, honest 52%.

Xiao is a wildcard with NO pro ranking: 14 years old (born 2012), ITF JUNIOR #414 (CH #391); her 2026 is J30/J60 titles in Asia plus first-round exits at J300 Pancevo and J200 Belgrade, and her ITF page lists hard as her preferred surface. Against her: 11-12 in 2026 and 0-4 in second/final qualifying rounds (Stosovic, Ghirardato, Hageman, Lukas), so she is beatable by anyone competent. On slow clay a 19-y-o with 60+ pro clay matches over a 14-y-o debutante should be ~59%, not 45c.

rows.tournament: Porto Open (CT Porto Cup) ATP Challenger, qualifying final, outdoor clay, Porto, Portugal (Aug 30-Sep 7)
rows.edge_summary: Schoen is 31-10 on hard in 2026 but 6-1 on clay, five of those in Swiss club league. First real clay test vs a man who played 30/30 matches on clay and made a Ch75 SF beating Dellien. Fuele ~43% at 39c.

edge_factors.detail: Schoen 2026: 31-10 hard, 6-1 clay - 5 of 6 clay wins are Swiss club league. Fuele: 30 of 30 matches in 2026 on clay; 125-79 career.

rows.headline: Pure clay grinder vs a hard-court M15 specialist on his 3rd clay start of 2026
rows.analysis: Porto Open qualifying final, outdoor clay. Schoen is the better player on paper: 37-11 in 2026 with two M15 Kayseri titles and an M25 Figueira da Foz final. But every one of those results came on hard court - he is 31-10 on hard this year and 6-1 on clay, and five of those six clay wins are Swiss Interclub club-league matches. His only competitive pro clay in 2026 is a 5-7 5-7 loss to Poljicak (#345) at Zug and yesterday's win over Boris Arias, a #1541 doubles specialist. He has never won a Challenger main-draw match. Fuele has played 30 of 30 matches in 2026 on clay (125-79 career) and six weeks ago qualified into the Cordenons Ch75 semis, beating top seed Hugo Dellien and Thiago Seyboth Wild. The counterweight is real: Fuele retired at M15 Xativa on Jul 30, lost 5-7 0-6 to #1043 Gavrielides at Augsburg on Aug 23, and needed 2h+ over three sets yesterday while Schoen spent 65 minutes. That, plus 27C heat, makes Schoen a deserved favourite - just not a 63c one. I make it 57/43; Fuele at 39c is the side with the price.
